**The Small Weather**

Every morning, the light arrives as if it has somewhere else to be. It slips across the floor, finds the dust, and makes a small country of it. For a few minutes, the room is full of distant stars. Then someone opens a door, the air changes, and the stars disappear. Nothing has been lost, exactly. The dust is still there, the floor is still there, and the morning continues. But the room has quietly become ordinary again, and we go on living in it without noticing how briefly it was a universe.

Perhaps most of life is like that: not a succession of grand discoveries but a series of things that almost become grand before we turn away. A cup warms the hands. A stranger holds a door. Rain taps the window with the patience of someone who knows we are listening, even when we pretend not to. We are forever standing at the edge of a meaning, called elsewhere by the kettle, the phone, the list of things that must be done before the day ends.

The lists are useful. They keep us from forgetting bread, birthdays, appointments, the names of medicines and the people who are waiting for us. But a list is a narrow sort of memory. It remembers what can be completed. It does not remember how your father sounded when he was trying not to laugh, or the exact blue of the hallway where you waited for news, or the friend who said, “Take your time,” and meant it. Those memories do not check themselves off. They remain unfinished, like a song heard through a wall.

I sometimes think we mistake unfinished things for failures. We want a clean ending: the apology accepted, the question answered, the old hurt neatly folded and placed somewhere sensible. We want to know what the long effort was for. But some things do not resolve. They loosen. The grip weakens; the thought returns less often. One day we discover that the story we have been carrying has changed its weight. We have not put it down. We have simply grown strong in a place we did not know was being exercised.

There is a tree outside my window that appears to be doing nothing. It stands through heat and rain, its branches lifting and lowering in the wind. In winter, it looks like a drawing made with a few dark strokes. In spring, it becomes extravagant. I have watched it for years and still cannot tell what it is thinking. This seems to me a generous quality. The tree does not explain itself. It offers shade, color, shelter for birds, and the quiet fact of its presence. Then it asks for nothing more than another season.

Human beings are less modest. We explain ourselves even when no one has asked. We tell stories about what we meant, what we planned, what we would have done if circumstances had been kinder. We make a case for our lives, as though some attentive judge were taking notes. Yet the people who love us often love us in the spaces between our explanations: when we are tired, when we forget the clever thing we meant to say, when we bring home the wrong kind of fruit and laugh about it. Love is frequently a witness that declines to testify.

When I was younger, I believed the future would arrive with a sound. A bell, perhaps, or the bright click of a lock turning. I imagined I would recognize the moment when I became the person I was supposed to be. Instead, the future came disguised as errands and ordinary Tuesdays. Years passed, and I found myself carrying groceries, answering messages, remembering which cupboard held the batteries. The grand transformation, if there was one, happened without announcing itself. I became someone by doing small things repeatedly, and by failing at some of them, and by trying again.

Maybe this is why we take photographs. Not because we think a picture can keep a moment alive, but because we know the moment will change even while we are inside it. We lift the camera to mark our helplessness. Here, we say. This was here. These people stood together in this light. One of them was looking away. Someone had just told a joke. The picture is not the day; it is a little window cut into the day, and when we look through it later, we see both what happened and everything the frame could not hold.

I wonder what would happen if we paid attention without trying to preserve anything. If we watched the steam rise from a bowl and let it vanish. If we listened to a person finish speaking before preparing our reply. If we accepted that a beautiful thing could be beautiful without becoming ours. Attention is not a net. It does not have to catch. Sometimes it is only the decision to stay in the room while the light moves across the floor.

Outside, the tree shifts in the evening wind. A bus sighs at the corner. Somewhere, a child is being called in for dinner. The world does not pause to explain its arrangements, and still it gives us these small invitations: a warm cup, a patch of sun, the familiar voice on the other end of the line. We can miss them, and often do. Then another morning comes, carrying its brief country of stars, and there is time—at least for a moment—to look.
